notes.text:
This is a mathematical proof draft of a sufficient geometric/density criterion, not a classification of S03. Its nonvacuity at zero threshold is proved in n2. Use dd^c=i∂bar∂/(2π), with ordinary wedge powers.

Let (X0,h0) be connected compact Hermitian of dimension m. Let Y=P^k, k≥1, carry normalized Fubini–Study κ with ∫Yκ^k=1. On X=X0×Y put H=h0+κ, N=m+k, C=binomial(N,m), V0=∫X0h0^m, and μ=(h0^m/V0)∧κ^k. Pullbacks are understood. For any smooth positive probability dV, put R=μ/dV. Thus R is smooth and bounded above and below by positive constants. Write F=f/R, so f dV=Fμ.

Fix 0<α<1 and o=[1:0:…:0]. Define, off o,
ψ=log(Σi≥1|zi|²/Σi≥0|zi|²), L=1−ψ, and u=1−L^α.
Set u(o)=−∞, its canonical value. In the chart z0=1 put r=Σi≥1|zi|²; then L=1−log(r/(1+r)). Define
 t=exp(1−L), a=αL^(α−1),
 Q=t+(1−t)a,
 D=t(1−a)+(1−t)α(1−α)L^(α−2),
 qα=Q^(k−1)D exp(k(L−1)).
This gives a smooth positive density on Y\{o}, including by smooth extension the hyperplane z0=0, where its value is 1−α. Below we prove MAκ^ext(u)=qακ^k, ∫qακ^k=1, and qα≥(1−α)^k.

For a fixed λ>0, the sufficient density condition is
 F(x,y)≤Aqα(y)exp(λ(L(y)^α−1))                                      (1)
almost everywhere off X0×{o}, for some finite A>0. Under (1), the genuine H-psh function
 sλ=u+(1/λ)log(CV0/A)                                               (2)
satisfies MAH^ext(sλ)≥exp(λsλ)f dV and has total mass exactly CV0. The supplied subsolution-to-greatest-solution implication therefore gives a greatest exact finite-mass solution. No positive individual threshold is required.

The hypothesis is an explicit density test, with no unknown potential. One useful growth formulation is the following. Put p=1+k(1−α). Suppose F is essentially bounded on every compact subset of X\(X0×{o}). If, for all sufficiently large L, uniformly essentially over x and the projective spheres,
 F(x,y)≤A′exp(k(L−1)+λL^α)L^(−p),                                 (3)
then (1) holds with another finite constant. In r coordinates, this is critical growth r^(−k), a logarithmic decay of power p, and an exp(λ|log r|^α) allowance.

For one density to pass for every λ>0, it suffices that F be locally essentially bounded off the displayed fiber and
 ess limsup(y→o) ess sup_x [log⁺(F(x,y)/qα(y))/L(y)^α]=0.             (4)
For a fixed λ, (4) bounds F/qα by exp((λ/2)L^α) near o. The remaining compact region has bounded ratio. Increasing a finite constant gives (1).

Genuine admissibility is established directly. For 0<ε≤1, define
 ψε=log((Σi≥1|zi|²+ε|z0|²)/Σi≥0|zi|²).
This is smooth, ≤0, and κ-psh: locally κ+dd^cψε is dd^c of the logarithm of a positive sum of squared holomorphic coordinates. The function χ(t)=1−(1−t)^α, t≤0, has 0<χ′≤α and χ″>0. Hence
 κ+dd^cχ(ψε)=(1−χ′)κ+χ′(κ+dd^cψε)+χ″dψε∧d^cψε≥(1−α)κ.
As ε decreases to zero, these smooth functions decrease to u. Near o, |u|=O(1+|log r|^α), which is locally integrable against smooth volume. The decreasing local psh-plus-smooth limit is therefore nontrivial, and the submean inequalities pass to it. It is the genuine canonical κ-psh function, with value −∞ at o. Its pullback is genuine H-psh. Adding the constant in (2) changes neither admissibility nor mass. No potential is modified on a null set.

The non-pluripolar measure and its mass can also be computed directly. On the affine chart, a local primitive of κ+dd^c u is
 Φ(r)=log(1+r)+1−[1−log(r/(1+r))]^α.
Differentiation gives rΦ′(r)=(r+αL^(α−1))/(1+r)=Q. The complex Hessian has tangential eigenvalue Φ′, repeated k−1 times, and radial eigenvalue Φ′+rΦ″=dQ/dr. Both are positive. Polar integration yields
 ∫{a<r<b}(dd^cΦ)^k=Q(b)^k−Q(a)^k.                                (5)
Indeed, the determinant is (Q/r)^(k−1)Q′ and radial smooth volume is a fixed constant times r^(k−1)dr. Its primitive is therefore a fixed constant times Q^k. The constant is one by comparison with the normalized Fubini–Study primitive log(1+r), whose flux is (r/(1+r))^k and whose total mass is one.

In the L coordinate, dQ/dL=−D. The radial Fubini–Study probability is k exp(−k(L−1))dL, oriented toward the pole. Thus (5) gives exactly qα above. Q tends to zero at r=0 and to one at infinity. The omitted hyperplane has zero smooth volume, and u is smooth there. On {u>−J}, max(u,−J) agrees with smooth u. These sets exhaust Y\{o}; the defining non-pluripolar exhaustion discards the pole and cutoff-level masses. Consequently
 MAκ^ext(u)=qακ^k,  ∫Yqακ^k=1.
This is a flux computation, not an inference of full mass from zero Lelong number. The strict positivity bound proves qα≥(1−α)^k off the pole.

On X\(X0×{o}), sλ is smooth. Factor dimensions give
 (H+dd^csλ)^N=C h0^m∧(κ+dd^cu)^k.
Using the same non-pluripolar exhaustion gives
 MAH^ext(sλ)=CV0qαμ, with mass CV0.                               (6)
No singular current is restricted to a fiber. Equations (1), (2), and (6) imply
 exp(λsλ)f dV≤(CV0/A)exp(λu)Aqαexp(−λu)μ=MAH^ext(sλ).
Both measures give zero mass to the polar fiber. This verifies the exact exponential coefficient.

As L→∞,
 Q~αL^(α−1), D~α(1−α)L^(α−2),
 qα~α^k(1−α)exp(k(L−1))L^(−1−k(1−α)).                            (7)
The radial density of qακ^k is
 W(L)=kQ^(k−1)D~kα^k(1−α)L^(−1−k(1−α)).
For every τ>0,
 exp(τ(L^α−1))W(L)→∞.                                           (8)
The logarithm is τL^α minus a fixed multiple of log L, which tends to infinity. Every punctured neighborhood of o therefore has infinite mass for qαexp(−τu)κ^k, although qακ^k has mass one. Relation (7) proves the comparison needed for (3).

If v−(h0)=0, then v−(H)=0. For any bounded genuine h0-psh v, the bounded product calculus gives
 MAH(v)=C MAh0(v)∧κ^k.
To verify the algebra, locally write h0+dd^cv=dd^c(v+ρ)+(h0−dd^cρ), with v+ρ bounded psh and ρ smooth. Expand the defining multilinear bounded products and smooth-background corrections. Pullback respects these expressions; degrees exceeding m on the base or k on the projective factor vanish. The only surviving total-degree N term has coefficient C. Pulling back bounded potentials with masses tending to zero proves the claim.

It proves solvability for a rigorously constructed choice in the concentration family, not for every allowed choice, and does not classify unrestricted S03.

Use the product notation of n1. Suppose the base has smooth strictly positive probability densities Fj relative to dV0=h0^m/V0 satisfying
 ch0(Fj)≤2^(−2j)/C.                                                (9)
We construct smooth strictly positive probabilities gj relative to κ^k such that
 fj(x,y)=R(x,y)Fj(x)gj(y),  f=Σj≥1 2^(−j)fj                        (10)
has integral one, is finite everywhere, is smooth off X0×{o}, and is bounded below by (1/2)minXf1>0. Its component scalars satisfy cH(fj)=Cch0(Fj)≤2^(−2j), so bH(f)=0. This one density has exponential subsolutions and greatest exact finite-mass solutions for every λ>0. All its exact exponential solutions are unbounded. If v−(h0)=0, n1 also gives v−(H)=0.

The construction works for every base sequence satisfying (9), by tailoring the projective densities to that sequence. It is not a theorem about arbitrary components already chosen on the full product.

There is an actual compact example. Take the supplied elliptic quotient X0=Ω/〈g〉, where Ω={[z:w]∈P^3:z,w∈C^2 are nonzero} and g[z:w]=[z:exp(2π)w]. Its supplied metric is
 h0=ω=α0+β0+dt∧d^ct,  t=log(‖w‖²/‖z‖²).
Background-P07 proves compactness, connectedness, positivity, V0=24π, and actual smooth potentials vl with h0+dd^cvl>0 and δl=∫(h0+dd^cvl)^3→0. Only those geometric and collapsing-potential conclusions are imported; its positive-threshold product densities are not used.

Choose a subsequence with δl≤2^(−2j)/C and define
 Fj=((h0+dd^cvl)^3/dV0)/δl.
These are smooth positive probabilities. The displayed equation and supplied uniqueness of the normalization scalar give ch0(Fj)=δl, proving (9). Thus the sequence needed here is available, rather than an unresolved premise. Taking k=1 gives a compact complex fourfold with C=4 and explicit subsolution mass CV0=96π. Taking k=2 gives subsolution mass 240π. These are not asserted masses of the greatest exact solutions.

Fix 0<α<1 once and for all and use u,L,qα from n1. Put
 wj=2^(−j), Mj=maxX0Fj, b0=(1−α)^k,
 Bτ(y)=qα(y)exp(τ(L(y)^α−1)).
Then Bτ≥b0, and its radial measure is exp(τ(L^α−1))W(L)dL, with W from n1.

Choose 0<εj≤1/2 such that
 wjεjMj≤b0 2^(−j−2).                                             (11)
Also impose wjεj‖Fj‖Cj≤2^(−j), using fixed smooth coordinate seminorms. Both conditions are possible for each smooth Fj. The baseline

then converges smoothly: for each fixed derivative order, all sufficiently large j are controlled by the second condition. It satisfies 0<E≤b0/4.

Choose one smooth cutoff ρ supported in [0,1], positive inside, flat at the endpoints, with 0≤ρ≤1; for example ρ(t)=exp(4−1/(t(1−t))) on (0,1), zero outside. Inductively choose Aj≥2 and Aj>Aj−1+2 such that

This choice is rigorously possible. For each fixed j, equation (8) of n1 shows that exp((L^α−1)/j)W(L) tends uniformly to infinity on [A,A+1] as A→∞. Since ∫ρ>0, the integral tends to infinity. Successive doubling gives a constructive search that terminates analytically. The annuli are disjoint and tend to the pole.

On the jth annulus define

and set it to zero outside. The annulus is compactly contained in Y\{o} and misses z0=0. Flatness of ρ makes extension by zero smooth. Each individual bump also vanishes on a neighborhood of o. It is radial, smooth globally, and has integral one by (12). Set

This is a smooth strictly positive probability. Moreover,

on its annulus. Different bump supports are disjoint.

We directly solve the smooth projective component equation, avoiding a new external existence theorem. For g=gj, set

It establishes solvability for tailored choices in the concentration family, not for every allowed choice. For n1, the smooth regularizations decrease to the stated canonical potential. The chain rule gives κ+dd^c u≥(1−α)κ, and local integrability prevents an identically minus-infinity limit. The pole value is the genuine canonical value. Direct differentiation gives rΦ′=Q and −dQ/dL=D. The normalized radial flux is Q(b)^k−Q(a)^k; its endpoint values are zero and one. Dividing its radial density by k exp(−k(L−1)) gives exactly the displayed qα. Its extension at the hyperplane has value 1−α, and the metric inequality gives qα≥(1−α)^k. Non-pluripolar truncation retains the smooth measure off the pole and discards cutoff and pole masses, so the projective mass is exactly one.

The product calculation retains the binomial coefficient C and the arbitrary reference-volume factor R. Local bounded-product expansion, followed by the specified non-pluripolar exhaustion, gives MA_ext_H(u)=CV0 qα μ with actual mass CV0. The shift λ^−1 log(CV0/A) yields precisely the requested coefficient λ. The asymptotic exponent is p=1+k(1−α), so the growth test (3) and the every-exponent test (4) imply (1). The attenuation allowance itself is not integrable: exp(τ(L^α−1))W(L) tends to infinity for each τ>0. The argument correctly keeps the separate L1 hypothesis on f. Pulling back bounded base potentials also proves v_−(H)=0 under the stated antecedent v_−(h0)=0.

For n2, each εj can satisfy both positive finite bounds. Using the usual cumulative C^j coordinate norms, these bounds imply smooth convergence of the baseline and E≤b0/4. For every fixed j, exponential growth dominates the polynomial decay of W uniformly on intervals [A,A+1]. Consequently Zj tends to infinity as A tends to infinity, and the induction can satisfy both (12) and the separation requirement for every j. Flat cutoff endpoints give globally smooth individual bumps. Each gj is strictly positive and has integral one.

The radial component equation is also valid globally. G′>0 gives positive tangential and radial eigenvalues. Near the origin its metric is εj^(1/k)κ. Near every infinity chart, v=|z0|²/Σi≥1|zi|² is smooth, the displayed derivative of φ is analytic in v, and the normal metric coefficient is εj while the tangential metric is κ. Thus φj is globally smooth and strictly admissible, including when k=1. The full product equation gives c_H(fj)=C c_h0(Fj), with no missing V0 or R factor. Probability, smooth positivity, and all required concentration inequalities hold for the full-product fj.

Tonelli gives integral f=1. The disjoint annuli are locally finite away from the polar fiber; on that fiber every bump vanishes and only the finite smooth baseline remains. Hence f is finite pointwise, smooth off the fiber, and uniformly positive through its first component. Threshold maximality gives a2^−j≤c_H(fj)≤2^−2j for every j, which excludes every positive scaled subsolution and proves b_H(f)=0.

The constructed f is independent of λ. For any λ>0, sufficiently late indices satisfy 1/j≤λ. Their masses are finite and positive because their potentials are bounded above and finite almost everywhere and f is positive and integrable. Their masses are not identified with CV0. Every exact solution is unbounded, since a bounded one would contradict the established zero threshold.

I independently checked the supplied quotient proof rather than treating background-P07 as a granted assumption. The deck action is free and properly discontinuous, and the compact strip proves compactness. The base forms and vertical form give a positive descended metric. The collapse argument is sound. A bounded subsequence of Cδ would meet Lamari’s nonnegative pairing hypothesis for Cω−Bδ, without requiring this form to be closed. Normalization, submean estimates propagated through a finite connected cover, and local compactness give a nontrivial canonical L1 limit. After adding local smooth corrections, the currents to which Siu is applied are positive and closed. Their Lelong level sets glue because smooth corrections have zero Lelong number. The divisor segment forces the entire connected plane minus two points into the lifted analytic set. Deck invariance then forces all Hk; their accumulation makes every local defining holomorphic function vanish identically, contradicting properness. This proves Cδ→infinity.

The remaining collapse estimates also check. Translation averaging has uniformly bounded degree and yields the required horizontal coefficient lower bound. The curve matrices have determinant bounded away from zero by 5/8, their deck translates are disjoint, and the evaluation map is a submersion at both projective-chart ends. This assignment is the restricted A–D reconstruction. Throughout, original_S03_completed=false. No necessity criterion, classification of all zero-threshold densities, or assertion for every previously chosen full-product concentration family is proved.

We use d^c=i(∂̄−∂)/(4π), hence dd^c=i∂∂̄/(2π). A genuine h-psh potential has its canonical upper representative, is locally psh plus smooth, satisfies h+dd^c u≥0, and is not identically −∞. Extended Monge–Ampère means the actual non-pluripolar measure obtained by restricting bounded truncations to {u>−T} and increasing T; poles receive no mass. Bounded products mean actual Bedford–Taylor products.

Three assertions explicitly supplied by the task are dependencies, not newly proved:

u=1−L^α, a=αL^(α−1), b=α(1−α)L^(α−2).

The variable v is also the globally smooth function ∑_{i≥1}|Z_i|²/∑_{i≥0}|Z_i|². It is zero precisely at o and equals one on the infinity hyperplane. Set u(o)=−∞, its canonical pole value.

κ+dd^c u=(1−a)κ+a(κ+dd^c ψ)+b dψ∧d^cψ.

The middle form is dd^c log r² on the affine chart, hence semipositive with tangential rank k−1. On any homogeneous-coordinate chart away from o it likewise has a local log-squared-norm potential and is semipositive. The last form is semipositive. Since a≤α<1, the whole form is ≥(1−α)κ and is smooth strictly positive off o.

At o, the local function P(s)=log(1+exp s)+u is genuinely psh. Its radial slopes are

p=P'(s)=v+a(1−v)>0,
P''(s)=(1−a)v(1−v)+b(1−v)^2>0.

These give tangential and radial Hessian positivity. P tends to −∞ at the origin and is locally integrable, with negative growth of order (log(1/r))^α. Exact density and normalization. For a radial P(log r²) on C^k\{0}, the complex Hessian eigenvalues are p/r² in k−1 tangential directions and P''/r² radially. With normalized spherical measure dσ, its top Monge–Ampère measure is

The constant follows from the exact dd^c: the Euclidean density is k!/π^k times the Hessian determinant, the sphere area is 2π^k/(k−1)!, and ds=2 dr/r. Applying this to log(1+r²), whose slope is v, gives ∫κ^k=[v^k]_0^1=1.

Since dL/ds=−(1−v), define

D=−dp/dL=(1−a)v+b(1−v)>0.

The positive radial density of κ^k with respect to dL dσ is k v^k. The Monge–Ampère radial density and its density relative to κ^k are therefore exactly

For every τ>0,

Thus e^(τ(L^α−1))W(L)→∞, and the allowance is not locally integrable near o:

Its ζ-support lies in an injective logarithmic neighbourhood. It is semipositive. On a fixed compact neighbourhood of these supports, σ_ζ≤Kω, so
0≤Bδ≤K||p||∞δ^{-2}ω.
Every normalized positive test therefore satisfies ∫BδΘ≤K||p||∞δ^{-2}. Thus Cδ is finite. Its test family is nonempty by Θ* from n1.

We first reconstruct the compactness needed below. On a connected compact complex manifold, genuine quasi-psh functions u_j with dd^c u_j≥−h for fixed smooth Hermitian h and sup u_j=0 have an L1-convergent subsequence. Choose finitely many relatively compact connected coordinate balls, with smaller cores covering the manifold. On each choose a bounded quadratic correction ρ with dd^cρ≥h. Then u_j+ρ is genuine psh. Subtracting a fixed upper bound for ρ gives a nonpositive subharmonic function w_j.

The maxima of u_j are attained. Pass to a subsequence whose maximum points converge to p. In a chart about p, w_j at those points has a uniform lower bound. Submean on fixed-radius balls centred there bounds ∫(−w_j); a fixed smaller ball about p lies in these balls for all sufficiently large j. This supplies an initial uniform L1 bound.

To propagate it, in a connected coordinate domain let S be the points having neighbourhoods with uniformly bounded ∫(−w_j). S is open. If x is in its relative closure, choose B(x,4r) inside the domain and a fixed ball A⊂S∩B(x,r/4). The bound on A supplies points a_j∈A with w_j(a_j)≥−M for one fixed finite M. Submean on B(a_j,r) bounds its integral of −w_j. Since B(x,r/2)⊂B(a_j,r), x∈S. Thus S is relatively closed and equals the connected coordinate domain. Finite coverings then bound every compact subset. Across overlapping charts, bounded corrections and bounded coordinate Jacobians on a smaller overlap transfer these bounds. The intersection graph of a connected finite coordinate cover is connected, so they propagate across the cover. The smaller cores give a global L1 bound. The permitted local psh compactness theorem, followed by finite diagonal extraction, gives local and global L1 convergence. Limits patch as distributions, and uniqueness of canonical psh representatives after smooth correction makes the limit genuine. This proves the required global normalized compactness.

Suppose δ_j→0 and C_{δ_j}≤M. Put κ=1/(M+1). For EVERY smooth strictly positive dd^c-closed test Θ, normalization by ∫ωΘ gives

The ordinary approximate-identity calculation in ζ gives

On each coordinate ball choose ρ=M|z|² with dd^cρ≥ω. The current R=dd^c(u+ρ) is CLOSED and positive and dominates κ[D_U] near that local divisor. Its geometric Lelong number there is at least κ. Lift A through the quotient covering to an analytic subset Ã⊂Ω. The hypersurface D0={w0=z0}∩Ω is connected: it is P2 with the two points where z=0 or w=0 removed. At P=[0:1:0:1]∈Ω use a=z0/z1, b=w0/z1 and r=w1/z1 near (0,0,1). Each Dm is b=q^m a. A local holomorphic defining function F of Ã has expansion F(a,b,r)=Σf_ij(r)a^i b^j. Vanishing on Dm gives, for every degree k and integer m,
